newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba says M3 grew faster than expected in early 97.
newsitem.headline: Buba says M3 grew faster than expected in early 97.

text.p: German M3 money supply rose more quickly than the Bundesbank had expected at the start of 1997, but it has not jeopardised price stability, the German central bank said in its monthly report for June on Wednesday.

M3, seen as a key policy tool and an indication of future inflation rates, was on average above the Bundesbank's expectations during the early part of this year. But "the existing price stability still does not appear to be in danger," the central bank report said.
The Bundesbank said fast M3 growth was mostly due to a large "statistical overhang" seen at the beginning of 1997.
Private-sector lending jumped late last year as borrowers scrambled to secure expiring tax advantages for construction in eastern Germany.

"After that, monetary expansion slowed markedly," the Bundesbank said. It noted M3, made up of cash in circulation, time, sight and short-term savings deposits, was at 6.7 percent in April and just above the 3.5- to 6.5-percent target rate.
During the first third of 1997, savings accounts grew most rapidly, the Bundesbank said. Cash in circulation and sight deposits also grew markedly, it said.
The slightly longer-term expanded M3, which includes money market funds, continued to grow more slowly than M3, the Bundesbank said.
"During the course of the last twelve months, (expanded M3) rose by around 5.5 percent compared with (a) rate of seven percent for M3," the Bundesbank said.
M3 developments reflect banks' reduced willingness to put money in longer-dated securities, the report said.

One reason monetary capital formation slipped again this year was the ongoing low level of capital market rates, the Bundesbank said. Another reason might have been uncertainty about upcoming monetary union, it said.

Between January and April, banks' monetary capital formation grew at a seasonally adjusted, annualised rate of four percent, compared with a rate of 5.5 percent in the four months before that, the central bank said.
The Bundesbank also said lending to banks and private individuals slowed during the first four months of 1997 to 56.3 billion marks ($32.5 billion) compared with 67.8 billion marks in 1996.

Translated into a seasonally-adjusted annualised rate, lending to banks and the private sector climbed at a seven-percent rate in the first four months of 1997 compared with an eight-percent increase in the last four months of 1996.

The central bank also said the markets now appear to expect unchanged interest rates for some time. It said monetary and economic conditions had argued for a steady course on interest rates over the last months.
Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke told Reuters on Tuesday there were few pressing reasons for an interest rate change and that rates would remain unchanged in the near-term.
The Bundesbank said it has been successful in fine-tuning its money market operations to the point where it did not need to resort to extraordinary measures during the first months of the year.
